title: Particle Physics and Gravitational Waves as complementary windows on the Universe
summary: Particle physics and gravitational waves provide complementary probes of the deep structure of the Universe. Gravitational waves from the mergers of neutron stars and black holes are sensitive to the structure of dense quark matter and to different dark matter scenarios. Measurements of stochastic gravitational waves backgrounds can teach us about possible first order phase transitions in the early Universe, including providing sensitivity to the TeV scale which is of key interest to future particle collider experiments. Gravitational waves measurements will also give new probes of the evolution and expansion of the Universe, complementary to measurements with electromagnetic radiation. This Perspectives article explores the physics synergies between the science opportunities provided by next generation gravitational waves measurements and particle physics experiments. Gravitational waves can also probe deep into the early Universe reaching physics much above possible collider energies if the signals can be detected.

AI.tldr: This article reviews how next generation gravitational wave observations complement particle physics experiments by probing dense matter, dark matter, early Universe phase transitions, and cosmic evolution, offering new windows into fundamental physics beyond collider energies.
AI.motivation: To explore the complementary insights gained from particle physics and gravitational wave observations in understanding the fundamental structure and evolution of the Universe.
AI.method: This paper discusses theoretical and observational approaches combining gravitational wave measurements from neutron star and black hole mergers, stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds, and comparisons with particle collider experiments to probe dense quark matter, dark matter, and early Universe phase transitions.
AI.result: The study highlights that gravitational waves provide unique sensitivity to dense matter structures, dark matter scenarios, first order phase transitions at the TeV scale, and cosmological evolution beyond electromagnetic methods, offering new synergies with particle physics research.
AI.conclusion: Gravitational wave measurements, together with particle physics experiments, offer complementary and unprecedented capabilities to probe fundamental physics from the TeV scale to energies beyond possible collider reach, enhancing our understanding of the deep structure and history of the Universe.

title: BLAZ4R and the eROSITA view of z>4 blazars
comment: Submitted to A&A. Catalog available at https://blaz4r.brera.inaf.it/
summary: We present BLAZ4R, the first living catalog of confirmed $z>4$ blazars, with a focus on the contribution of eROSITA, on board of the Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG) spacecraft. Blazars at $z>4$ are rare but powerful probes of how active supermassive black holes evolve in connection to relativistic jets, in the first 2 billion years of cosmic history. At these redshifts, X-ray observations are essential for constraining blazars jet power and orientation, enabling effective trace of their parent population. The all-sky surveys provided by eROSITA ensure X-ray detection for BLAZ4R sources and, in some cases, allow spectral and temporal studies of their jetted emission. BLAZ4R includes 54 confirmed blazars, characterized through their X-ray properties, radio spectra and morphology, and multiwavelength profiles. We confirm that jetted sources are significantly more numerous relative to non-jetted counterparts at high-$z$, and that blazars (and therefore the overall jetted population) do not exhibit significantly different features compared to the total active galactic nuclei population in the early Universe. Fast accretion processes that involve relativistic jets are clearly required to justify the existence of fully formed jetted AGN at $z>4$. However, the diverse multiwavelength properties characterizing BLAZ4R do not yet allow us to identify the specific signatures of these processes. We will continue updating BLAZ4R to search for such signatures and ultimately understand the early formation of jetted AGN.

AI.tldr: BLAZ4R is the first catalog of confirmed $z>4$ blazars, leveraging eROSITA X-ray data to study their jets and evolution. It finds more jetted sources at high redshift but no distinct early-Universe AGN features, highlighting the need for ongoing observations to understand early jet formation.
AI.motivation: To understand how active supermassive black holes with relativistic jets evolve within the first 2 billion years of cosmic history, focusing on rare blazars at redshift greater than 4.
AI.method: Compiling and analyzing the first living catalog (BLAZ4R) of 54 confirmed $z>4$ blazars, utilizing X-ray data from the eROSITA all-sky surveys aboard the SRG spacecraft, combined with multiwavelength profiles including radio spectra and morphology to characterize blazars and their jet properties.
AI.result: Identified that jetted sources are significantly more numerous relative to non-jetted AGN at high redshift, with blazars showing no significant difference compared to the overall AGN population in the early Universe. Fast accretion processes involving relativistic jets are necessary to explain these fully formed jetted AGN at $z>4$, though specific signatures of these processes remain undetected so far.
AI.conclusion: BLAZ4R provides a critical resource for tracing the evolution of jetted AGN at high redshift; continued updates and observations are needed to identify definitive signatures of early relativistic jet formation and accretion processes in the early Universe.

title: Systematic Monitoring of Extreme X-ray Variability from Weak-line Quasars
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present the results of a multi-cycle Chandra program to systematically monitor the X-ray variability of 10 weak-line quasars (WLQs) that previously had limited multi-epoch X-ray observations. Three new Chandra 2.8 to 8.2 ks observations were obtained for each WLQ with C$\,$IV rest-frame equivalent widths (REWs) $\lesssim 10$ Å, substantially improving the monitoring data quality of WLQs and our ability to characterize their long-term X-ray variability behavior. We observe recurrent extreme X-ray variability in the historically variable WLQ SDSS J1539+3954, with an X-ray flux rise of a factor of $\gtrsim 6$ between 2023 and 2024 ($\gtrsim 21$ relative to 2013). Another previously X-ray weak WLQ in the sample, SDSS J0825+1155, underwent a significant X-ray flux variation by a factor of $\gtrsim 14$ between 2019 and 2023. We find the fraction of WLQs exhibiting evidence of extreme X-ray variability to be $0.20^{+0.17}_{-0.07}$. In the context of the thick disk and outflow (TDO) model, the substantial fraction of WLQs displaying extreme X-ray variability may suggest that the variability is driven by the intrinsic motion of the TDO wind rather than changes in the height of the TDO disk. We performed a statistical comparison between the distribution of variability amplitudes of WLQs and general radio-quiet quasars. We find that these underlying distributions are statistically different, with WLQs having $\approx 6.8$ times higher odds of exhibiting an extreme X-ray variability event than the general radio-quiet quasar population.

AI.tldr: Systematic Chandra monitoring of WLQs reveals a significant fraction exhibit extreme long-term X-ray variability markedly more frequent than in typical quasars, likely caused by intrinsic TDO wind dynamics.
AI.motivation: To improve the understanding of X-ray variability behavior in WLQs, which had limited multi-epoch X-ray observations previously, specifically to quantify the frequency and amplitude of extreme variability events.
AI.method: Multi-cycle Chandra X-ray monitoring with 2.8 to 8.2 ks exposures for a sample of 10 weak-line quasars (WLQs) with C IV REWs less than 10 Å to characterize long-term X-ray variability.
AI.result: Recurrent extreme X-ray variability detected in notable WLQs, such as SDSS J1539+3954 with flux changes exceeding factors of 6 to 21 over years; at least 20% of WLQs show extreme variability. Statistical comparison indicates WLQs have about 6.8 times higher odds of extreme X-ray variability than general radio-quiet quasars. These findings favor a variability mechanism tied to intrinsic motion of the thick disk and outflow (TDO) wind rather than structural height changes.
AI.conclusion: Extreme X-ray variability is prevalent among WLQs and statistically distinct from general quasar variability, supporting the thick disk and outflow model with intrinsic wind motion as the primary driver of variability.

title: The background gas humming and multi-messenger transients of stalled supermassive black hole binaries
summary: We establish the multi-messenger mechanics of episodic mass transfer in supermassive black hole binaries stalled within circumbinary discs. Utilizing continuous wavelet transforms, we isolate localized gas clumps at the cavity edge and track their evolution. By regularizing the forced fluid equations at Lindblad resonances via the inhomogeneous Airy differential equation, we bypass linear singularities to extract the finite wave amplitudes that trigger non-linear shock formation. These shocks produce bounded accretion bursts. We model the time-domain thermal luminosity, deriving an analytical power spectral density that forms a harmonic cascade. The superposition of the accretion streams generates a spectral beat frequency, providing an exact mathematical extraction of the binary mass ratio. The radiative cooling of shock-accelerated electrons produces a multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution from a synchrotron radio continuum to an inverse-Compton gamma-ray tail. We identify a relativistic signature: a discontinuous, high-frequency gravitational wave sideband termed the ``background gas humming''. This emission arises from the highly asymmetric, transient fluid geometry of the accretion shocks. Evaluating the asymptotic properties of the Airy regularization, we show that this humming manifests as a sequence of discrete high-frequency bursts with temporal quiescence gaps that systematically compress as the cavity shrinks. We show that the instantaneous mass of the gas actively trapped within the cavity violently amplifies prior to decoupling, culminating in a terminal burst near 4.0 mHz that serves as a multi-messenger precursor to the final vacuum inspiral.

AI.tldr: The paper models the fluid and radiative dynamics of episodic mass transfer in supermassive black hole binaries, revealing accretion burst signatures and a novel gravitational wave phenomenon ('background gas humming') that provide new multi-messenger precursors to black hole mergers.
AI.motivation: To develop a comprehensive, multi-messenger theoretical framework connecting fluid dynamics and radiative signatures of episodic mass transfer in supermassive black hole binaries stalled within circumbinary disks, providing novel observational diagnostics and gravitational wave signatures preceding the final merger.
AI.method: 'Continuous wavelet transforms' are employed to isolate localized gas clumps; fluid dynamics at Lindblad resonances are regularized using the inhomogeneous Airy differential equation to bypass singularities and extract finite wave amplitudes triggering shock formation; analytical modeling of thermal luminosity and power spectral density; radiative processes modeled to produce multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution; asymptotic analysis of Airy regularization to characterize gravitational wave emissions.
AI.result: Identification of localized gas clumps driving non-linear shocks producing bounded accretion bursts; derivation of an analytical power spectral density showing harmonic cascades and a spectral beat frequency enabling exact binary mass ratio extraction; prediction of a multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution from shock-accelerated electrons; discovery of a novel gravitational wave sideband ('background gas humming') characterized by discrete high-frequency bursts linked to fluid asymmetries; elucidation of a terminal burst near 4.0 mHz as a precursor to the vacuum inspiral phase.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that episodic mass transfer in supermassive black hole binaries generates distinct multi-messenger signals, including accretion bursts, spectral signatures enabling binary mass ratio extraction, and unique gravitational wave sidebands termed 'background gas humming,' which act as precursors to the final merger phase.

title: CMB constraints on dark matter-proton scattering: investigating prior-volume effects using profile likelihoods
summary: We present profile-likelihood constraints on velocity-independent dark matter-proton scattering, including cases in which only a fraction of dark matter has such non-gravitational interactions. Frequentist profile-likelihood techniques provide prior-independent constraints, circumventing prior-volume effects that we show arise in Bayesian constraints on this model. In the limit where the scattering cross section or the fraction of interacting dark matter approaches zero, the other interacting dark matter model parameters become unconstrained, causing the posterior distribution to favor that region of parameter space. Using Planck 2018 cosmic microwave background anisotropy data, we find a clear impact of prior-volume effects on the posteriors used to place constraints on dark matter scattering. Compared to the frequentist analysis, the Bayesian method consistently overestimates the constraints on the cross section. Given the potentially biased upper limits on models subject to prior-volume effects, such as this one, we recommend supplementing Bayesian constraints with frequentist statistics to better assess the impact of priors.

AI.tldr: This paper uses frequentist profile-likelihood methods on Planck 2018 data to avoid prior-volume biases found in Bayesian analyses of dark matter-proton scattering, recommending frequentist approaches to improve constraint reliability.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of Bayesian methods in constraining dark matter-proton scattering parameters due to prior-volume effects, which bias upper limit estimates.
AI.method: Applied frequentist profile-likelihood techniques to analyze velocity-independent dark matter-proton scattering using Planck 2018 CMB anisotropy data, comparing results to Bayesian approaches.
AI.result: Frequentist analysis provides prior-independent constraints, revealing that Bayesian methods overestimate constraints on the dark matter scattering cross section due to prior-volume effects, especially when parameters approach zero.
AI.conclusion: Frequentist statistics should complement Bayesian constraints to mitigate biases from prior-volume effects in dark matter scattering models, leading to more reliable parameter constraints.

title: Parameterizing Dark Energy at the density level: A two-parameter alternative to CPL
comment: 23 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables. Comments are welcome!
summary: We introduce a minimal two-parameter formulation of the dark energy (DE) density evolution normalized to its present-day value, $f_{\rm DE}(z) \equiv ρ_{\rm DE}(z)/ρ_{\rm DE,0}$, in terms of $f_p\equiv f_{\rm DE}(z_p)$ and the DE equation of state $w_p\equiv w(z_p)$, at a pivot redshift $z_p$. This provides an alternative framework for assessing the evidence for evolving DE, complementary to the established Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) parameterization. By parameterizing the DE density directly, the $(w_p,\,f_p)$ formulation avoids the approximate degeneracies intrinsic to the $(w_0,\,w_a)$ basis -- in particular the weak sensitivity of the expansion history to $w_a$ -- while reproducing the background evolution of representative quintessence models with equivalent accuracy. Confronting it with the latest baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements from DESI, a prior on early-universe parameters from Planck cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations, and Type Ia supernovae (SNe) data, we find that the $w_p$ and $f_p$ parameters are both tightly constrained and sensitive to distinct subsets of the data. Specifically, $w_p$ is measured to percent-level precision by BAO and CMB alone, while $f_p$ is pinned down by the independent matter density constraint that only SNe provide. Including the Pantheon+ SNe sample, we obtain $w_p = -1.04 \pm 0.04$ and $f_p = 1.07 \pm 0.04$, with similar results when using the DESY5 SNe sample. The preference for evolving DE over $Λ$CDM remains below $3σ$ across all dataset combinations, comparable to that obtained with CPL. Notably, the proximity of both $w_p$ and $f_p$ to their cosmological constant values of $(-1,1)$ -- precisely at the epoch where the data are most sensitive -- deepens the coincidence previously identified in the CPL framework, reinforcing the case for caution in interpreting the current evidence for dynamical DE.

AI.tldr: A new two-parameter dark energy density parameterization avoids shortcomings of the CPL model, fits current cosmological data well, and finds no significant evidence for evolving dark energy, with parameters near the cosmological constant values.
AI.motivation: To provide a complementary and potentially more robust framework for probing evolving dark energy by directly parameterizing the dark energy density, thus avoiding the degeneracies and weak sensitivities associated with the CPL parameterization, especially regarding $w_a$.
AI.method: The paper introduces a minimal two-parameter model of dark energy density evolution parameterized directly in terms of $f_p$ and $w_p$ at a pivot redshift $z_p$, as an alternative to the CPL $(w_0, w_a)$ parameterization. This model is confronted with the latest data from DESI BAO, Planck CMB priors, and Type Ia supernovae (Pantheon+ and DESY5).
AI.result: The parameters $w_p$ and $f_p$ are tightly constrained by distinct data sources; $w_p$ by BAO and CMB, and $f_p$ by supernovae. Best-fit values $w_p = -1.04 \\pm 0.04$ and $f_p = 1.07 \\pm 0.04$ are close to the cosmological constant values $(-1,1)$, with no significant preference for dark energy evolution over standard $\Lambda$CDM.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the two-parameter $(w_p, f_p)$ formulation provides tight constraints on dark energy parameters that are close to the cosmological constant model, showing no strong evidence for evolving dark energy beyond $3σ$. This reinforces cautious interpretation of current data suggesting dynamical dark energy.

title: Production of heavy $α$-elements and $^{44}$Ti in Cas A: comparison to abundances from 1D core-collapse supernova models and evidence for Carbon-Oxygen shell mergers
summary: The merger between the carbon (C) and oxygen (O) shells hours to days before the collapse of a massive star significantly changes its nucleosynthesis, which is reflected in the elemental ratios observed in supernova remnants (SNRs). We present a nucleosynthesis study of $^{44}$Ti production in core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), highlighting large silicon (Si), sulfur (S), calcium (Ca), and, most importantly, argon (Ar) to neon (Ne) ratios as diagnostics for carbon-oxygen (C--O) shell mergers. We compare yields from eight different sets of CCSNe models to observations of Cassiopeia A (Cas A), and show that C--O shell mergers are consistently the models that best match X-ray and infrared observations. These models produce high Ar/Ne ratios ($\gtrsim 0.1$), due to $^{20}$Ne depletion and production of $^{36}$Ar and $^{38}$Ar, while lower ratios are obtained from non-merger cases. Based on the Ar/Ne diagnostic, we compare the range of expected $^{44}$Ti produced by C--O shell mergers, which is up to $\sim 20 - 30 \%$ of the overall $^{44}$Ti, but expected to be located outside the reverse shock. Based on the sets of models considered, the photon flux expected from the $^{44}$Ti synthesized in the C--O shell merger in Cas A is below the $NuSTAR$ and $COSI$ detection limits, compatible with current limits locating most of the $^{44}$Ti interior to the reverse shock, but might be detectable from proposed missions like $ASCENT$. Finally, for the SNR of 1987A, a dominant C--O merger origin of the observed $^{44}$Ti is unlikely based on the observed redshift in its $^{44}$Ti line.

AI.tldr: This study shows that carbon-oxygen shell mergers in massive star supernovae enhance certain elemental ratios and contribute significantly to $^{44}$Ti production. Models including these mergers best explain observations in Cassiopeia A, while SN 1987A likely has a different $^{44}$Ti origin. Current instruments cannot detect all $^{44}$Ti contributions, but future missions might.
AI.motivation: To understand how the merger between the carbon and oxygen shells before the collapse of massive stars influences nucleosynthesis, particularly the production of $^{44}$Ti, and how this affects elemental ratios observable in supernova remnants.
AI.method: Conducted a nucleosynthesis study focusing on $^{44}$Ti production by comparing yields from eight different sets of core-collapse supernova models, especially analyzing elemental ratios like Ar/Ne. These results were compared with X-ray and infrared observations of supernova remnants such as Cassiopeia A and SN 1987A.
AI.result: Models incorporating carbon-oxygen shell mergers best match observed high Ar/Ne ratios and predicted $^{44}$Ti yields. The $^{44}$Ti produced in such mergers accounts for up to 20-30% of total $^{44}$Ti but is located outside the reverse shock, making it currently undetectable by NuSTAR and COSI but potentially detectable by future missions like ASCENT. The observed $^{44}$Ti redshift in SN 1987A suggests a different origin than a dominant C-O shell merger.
AI.conclusion: Carbon-oxygen shell mergers prior to core-collapse significantly impact nucleosynthesis signatures, particularly increasing Ar/Ne ratios and contributing a notable fraction of $^{44}$Ti. Observations of Cas A support merger models, while SN 1987A data suggest alternative scenarios. Future observations may further clarify $^{44}$Ti distributions and their origins.

title: Investigation on the X-ray emission of NGC 4051 during its 2009 optical/UV-X-ray dissociation phase
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: This study investigates the X-ray characteristics of jet-associated radio-quiet AGNs across distinct optical/UV to X-ray correlation phases. Quasi-simultaneous optical/UV/X-ray observations of NGC 4051 from May-June 2009, obtained through Swift and XMM-Newton, reveal a temporal dichotomy: a strong optical/UV to X-ray correlation dominates the initial observation phase (before May 27), followed by an optical/UV flare event concurrent with X-ray flux suppression in the latter period. Our multi-method analysis of XMM-Newton data, incorporating short-term X-ray variability assessment, spectral decomposition, and RGS spectral analysis, identifies significant inter-phase X-ray emission disparities. During optical/UV flaring episodes, compared to the correlated phase, we observe: attenuated short-term X-ray variability amplitudes, enhanced soft X-ray absorption, suppressed intrinsic hard X-ray flux, and more prominent RGS emission-line features. Notably, these X-ray characteristics during optical/UV flaring intervals show no statistically significant deviations from pre-flare low-state X-ray emission patterns. These non-synchronous optical/UV-X-ray variations contradict predictions from both reprocessing models, starburst-driven emission scenarios, and the simplistic absorption models. While potential jet-related mechanisms remain ambiguous, our findings demonstrate strong consistency with predictions from the inhomogeneous accretion disk perturbation framework.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes X-ray and optical/UV observations of NGC 4051, revealing distinct phases with correlated and anti-correlated variability. The findings challenge simple emission and absorption models, favoring an inhomogeneous accretion disk perturbation as the key driver of variability in jet-associated radio-quiet AGNs.
AI.motivation: To investigate the X-ray characteristics of jet-associated radio-quiet AGNs during different optical/UV to X-ray correlation phases and understand the underlying physical processes driving these variations.
AI.method: Quasi-simultaneous optical/UV/X-ray observations of NGC 4051 using Swift and XMM-Newton from May-June 2009 were conducted, followed by a multi-method analysis of XMM-Newton data involving short-term X-ray variability assessment, spectral decomposition, and Reflection Grating Spectrometer (RGS) spectral analysis.
AI.result: A temporal dichotomy was observed: initially strong optical/UV to X-ray correlation followed by an optical/UV flare with concurrent X-ray flux suppression. During flaring, X-ray variability amplitudes were reduced, soft X-ray absorption increased, intrinsic hard X-ray flux was suppressed, and RGS emission-line features became more prominent, with these features resembling pre-flare low-state X-ray emissions. The observed asynchronous optical/UV and X-ray changes contradict several existing models but align with the inhomogeneous accretion disk perturbation framework.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the complex X-ray and optical/UV variability patterns in NGC 4051 are inconsistent with simple reprocessing, starburst, or absorption models, and instead strongly support the inhomogeneous accretion disk perturbation model as the underlying mechanism for the observed phenomena.

title: The 'Forgotten' Neutrons: Implications for the Propagation of High-Energy Cosmic Rays in Magnetized Astrophysical and Cosmological Structures
comment: 39 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in Universe special issue: Studying Astrophysics with High-Energy Cosmic Particles
summary: Cosmological filaments, galaxy clusters, and galaxies are magnetized reservoirs of cosmic rays (CRs). The exchange of CRs across these structures is usually modeled assuming that they remain charged and magnetically confined. At high energies, hadronic interactions can convert CR protons to neutrons. This physics is routinely included in air-shower and ultra-high-energy (UHE) CR propagation Monte Carlo simulations used for composition studies but is rarely treated explicitly in propagation models of CR transport and exchange between magnetized reservoirs. CR neutrons are not affected by magnetic fields and can propagate ballistically over kpc-Mpc distances before decaying back into protons, with relativistic time dilation extending their effective decay length. We show how such charged-neutral switching modifies CR confinement and escape in four representative environments: a Milky Way-like galaxy, a starburst galaxy, a galaxy cluster, and a cosmological filament. By solving the transport of a confined CR proton population in each structure using a diffusion/streaming propagation approach with hadronic pp and p$γ$ interactions, and treating neutron production and decay as a stochastic Poisson ''jump'' process, we find that neutron-mediated steps can allow additional CR escape from large-scale cosmological structures at energies where charged-particle transport alone would predict strong CR confinement and attenuation in ambient radiation fields. These effects imply a qualitative shift in how ultra-high-energy CRs are transferred from embedded sources into filaments and voids once intermediate neutron propagation is considered, with consequences for the partitioning of CRs across the large-scale structure of the Universe.

AI.tldr: This study incorporates neutron production and decay into cosmic ray transport models in galaxies and clusters, showing that neutrons enable ultra-high-energy cosmic rays to escape more effectively from magnetized structures than previously thought, reshaping our understanding of cosmic ray distribution in the Universe.
AI.motivation: To address the incomplete modeling of cosmic ray (CR) transport between magnetized cosmic structures by including high-energy CR proton to neutron conversion effects, which are often neglected in CR propagation models but relevant for understanding CR confinement and escape.
AI.method: The study models CR transport in four cosmic environments (Milky Way-like galaxy, starburst galaxy, galaxy cluster, cosmological filament) by solving transport equations for CR protons using diffusion/streaming approaches combined with hadronic pp and pγ interaction terms, and incorporates neutron production and decay as a stochastic Poisson 'jump' process allowing for charged-neutral switching.
AI.result: Neutron-mediated transport allows cosmic rays to escape more effectively from large-scale structures at ultra-high energies than predicted by charged particle transport alone, altering qualitative expectations of CR confinement and attenuation and impacting CR distribution across cosmic structures.
AI.conclusion: Including neutron production and decay in CR transport models reveals that intermediate neutron propagation fundamentally modifies ultra-high-energy CR escape from magnetized cosmic environments and affects the distribution and exchange of CRs across the Universe's large-scale structure.

title: Constraints on the Physical Association between ICECAT1 Neutrinos and Fast Radio Bursts Using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalogue
summary: We present a search for neutrino counterparts to fast radio bursts (FRBs) using temporal and spatial cross-matching between the Second CHIME/FRB catalogue and the IceCube high-energy alert-track catalogue ICECAT1. Because current FRB--neutrino models do not provide a unique consensus on emission ordering, our primary significance test adopts a two-sided, order-agnostic temporal hypothesis. The analysis accounts for declination-dependent CHIME/FRB exposure and the look-elsewhere effect across multiple trials. No statistically significant FRB--neutrino association is found. The most significant pair is FRB\,20190630C--IC\,190629A, with a post-trial probability of $p=0.076$ ($1.43σ$), consistent with a chance coincidence. Within our statistical framework, a detectable physical association would require a time offset shorter than $\sim256$~s at $3σ$ or $\sim63$~ms at $5σ$. Using a population-level stacking analysis, we derive 90\% upper limits on the neutrino-to-radio luminosity ratio of FRBs, $ξ\lesssim 10^{8}-10^{11}$ for neutrino power-law spectral indices $γ=1.0-3.0$. These limits improve upon previous constraints by approximately two orders of magnitude and represent the most stringent bounds from FRB--neutrino coincidence searches to date. Although the current limits remain above the predictions of most magnetar-based models, they begin to constrain scenarios involving exceptionally efficient hadronic energy dissipation.

AI.tldr: This study searched for neutrino signals coincident with FRBs but found no significant associations. It sets stringent new limits on neutrino emission from FRBs, thereby constraining some theoretical models.
AI.motivation: To investigate potential neutrino counterparts to fast radio bursts (FRBs) given the uncertain emission ordering in current models.
AI.method: Temporal and spatial cross-matching of the CHIME/FRB catalogue with the IceCube high-energy neutrino alert catalogue, using an order-agnostic temporal hypothesis and accounting for declination exposure and multiple trials.
AI.result: No statistically significant FRB--neutrino associations were found; the strongest candidate was consistent with chance. Population-level stacking provided tight upper limits on neutrino-to-radio luminosity ratios, improving previous constraints by about two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Current data do not support a significant association between FRBs and neutrinos, but new constraints begin to challenge some models involving highly efficient hadronic processes in FRBs.

title: X-ray spectral and temporal evolution of atoll source 4U 1820-30 with AstroSat: detection of high frequency quasi-periodic oscillation
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures, Accepted for Publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: AstroSat/LAXPC and SXT observed the persistent neutron star low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1820-30 between 2016 and 2022. During these observations, the hardness-intensity diagram (HID) and color-color diagram (CCD) indicated that the source was in the banana state. We divided the CCD into 11 segments for spectral and timing analyses. For each segment in the CCD, we modeled the spectral data using two distinct approaches over the 0.7-20.0 keV band. A combination of a multi-color-disk component with an inner disk temperature of around 0.6 keV and Comptonized emission from the boundary layer (BL)/ hot corona provided the best description of the X-ray spectral data of this source. The truncation radius was found to be in the range of $\sim$ 19-40 km. The Comptonized component has an optical depth in the range of $\sim 7 - 13$ with electron temperature in the range of $\sim 2.5 - 3.8$ keV. The optical depth of the corona varies significantly along the position on the CCD, while $\sim$ 80\% of the X-ray flux comes from the Comptonized component. We discuss possible physical scenarios to explain the relationship between the spectral evolution and motion of the source along the CCD. The timing analysis revealed kHz QPOs peaks at $\sim 710$ Hz and $\sim 740$ Hz in the lower left banana branch. An energy-dependent study indicates that these QPOs are stronger in the high-energy band.

AI.tldr: AstroSat observations of 4U 1820-30 show it in the banana state with spectral data best described by a multi-color disk plus Comptonized emission. The corona's optical depth varies along the source's CCD position, dominating X-ray flux. kHz QPOs at ~710 and ~740 Hz appear in low banana states and are stronger at higher energies.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectral and timing properties of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1820-30 during its banana state using AstroSat observations.
AI.method: Observations from AstroSat/LAXPC and SXT were used to study 4U 1820-30 between 2016 and 2022. The hardness-intensity and color-color diagrams divided the source states into 11 segments for detailed spectral and timing analysis. Spectral modeling was performed over 0.7-20.0 keV using a multi-color-disk component and Comptonized emission from the boundary layer or corona. Timing analysis focused on kHz quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs).
AI.result: The source was consistently in the banana state with a disk inner temperature around 0.6 keV and a truncation radius between 19-40 km. The Comptonized component dominated (~80% flux) with optical depth varying from 7 to 13 and electron temperature 2.5-3.8 keV. QPOs at ~710 Hz and ~740 Hz were found in the lower left banana branch, stronger at high energies. The optical depth variations correlated with the source's position on the CCD.
AI.conclusion: Spectral evolution and timing features of 4U 1820-30 in the banana state are explained by changes in the Comptonizing corona's optical depth and electron temperature, coupled with the accretion disk properties. The presence of kHz QPOs linked to high-energy bands supports models involving the boundary layer or corona dynamics.

title: Binary neutron star mergers with a subsolar mass star
summary: While there are a number of proposed formation channels for subsolar mass compact objects, including black holes formed primordially, or neutron stars that form in collapsar disks, there have yet to be any conclusive observations of such objects. Motivated by the possibility that, if such objects exist, gravitational waves from binary mergers may reveal them, we study binary neutron star mergers where one star has a subsolar-mass in order to determine how well such systems are described by current models, and when they could be distinguished from a system with a subsolar-mass black hole. We perform fully general-relativistic simulations of a $1.7\ M_{\odot}$ star merging with a $0.8\ M_{\odot}$ star, leading to tidal deformabilities of up to $\mathcal{O}(10^4)$ for the latter, and quantify how this affects the merger dynamics and associated gravitation and electromagnetic signals. In this regime, we find mass transfer between the stars, as well as significantly lower disruption frequencies. Though this is not captured by current gravitational waveform models, we conclude that this does not significantly impact the sensitivity of current gravitational wave detectors to these sources. Assuming design sensitivity of the LIGO and Virgo detectors, we find no biases in the recovered intrinsic parameters for signal-to-noise ratios $\lesssim 100$. We also find that the large deformabilities lead to a significant increase in the amount of dynamically ejected matter compared to equal mass systems, exceeding the predictions of current phenomenological models.

AI.tldr: Simulations of neutron star mergers with one subsolar mass companion show mass transfer and large tidal effects not in current waveform models, but LIGO/Virgo sensitivity and parameter recovery remain robust. Ejecta mass is significantly higher than expected, implying stronger electromagnetic signals.
AI.motivation: There is interest in identifying and understanding subsolar mass compact objects, such as primordial black holes or neutron stars formed in unusual environments, which have not been conclusively observed yet. Gravitational waves from binary mergers could potentially reveal their existence.
AI.method: Fully general-relativistic simulations of binary neutron star mergers involving a 1.7 solar mass star and a 0.8 solar mass star were conducted to model the dynamics and resulting gravitational and electromagnetic signals, focusing on effects of extreme tidal deformabilities.
AI.result: The simulations revealed mass transfer during merger, lower disruption frequencies, and significantly increased dynamically ejected matter compared to equal mass systems. Current gravitational waveform models do not capture all these effects, but there is no significant impact on detector sensitivity or parameter estimation bias for SNRs below 100 at design LIGO/Virgo sensitivities.
AI.conclusion: Despite discrepancies with waveform models, gravitational wave detectors like LIGO and Virgo can accurately detect and parameterize mergers involving subsolar mass neutron stars without bias at moderate SNRs. The increased ejecta mass suggests enhanced electromagnetic signals, which current models underestimate.

title: Jet Power Estimates of FSRQs PKS 1441+25 and Ton 599 from Broadband SED Modeling
summary: Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs) are among the most energetic and powerful active galactic nuclei, often exhibiting jet powers comparable to or exceeding the Eddington luminosity. In this work, we performed broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling of two FSRQs PKS 1441+25 and Ton 599, using Swift-XRT/UVOT, NuSTAR, Fermi-LAT and VERITAS observations during 2015 and 2021, respectively. We considered four particle distribution models: a broken power law, a log-parabola, and two energy-dependent models in which either the diffusion or acceleration timescale depends on energy. Our results show that the jet power estimates derived from models with intrinsic curvature, such as the log-parabola and energy-dependent models, are of the same order as those obtained with a broken power-law distribution. This contrasts with the case of High Synchrotron Peaked Blazars (HBLs), where the power estimates can differ by nearly two orders of magnitude between models. We attribute this difference to the lower electron break energies typically observed in FSRQs. Consequently, our findings suggest that, unlike in HBLs, the estimated jet powers in FSRQs are relatively insensitive to the assumed particle energy distribution, reflecting the dominance of external Compton processes and weaker dependence on spectral curvature.

AI.tldr: This paper models the spectral energy distributions of two powerful FSRQs with multiple particle distribution models, finding that jet power estimates are robust across models. Unlike HBLs, FSRQ jet powers are less sensitive to spectral curvature due to their lower electron break energies and dominant external Compton processes.
AI.motivation: To understand how different particle distribution models affect jet power estimates in Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs) and compare these effects to those in High Synchrotron Peaked Blazars (HBLs).
AI.method: Broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling was performed on two FSRQs (PKS 1441+25 and Ton 599) using multiwavelength observations from Swift-XRT/UVOT, NuSTAR, Fermi-LAT, and VERITAS. Four particle distribution models were considered: broken power law, log-parabola, and two energy-dependent models involving diffusion or acceleration timescales dependent on energy.
AI.result: Jet power estimates from models incorporating intrinsic curvature (log-parabola and energy-dependent models) are similar in magnitude to those from broken power-law models for FSRQs. This contrasts with HBLs, where different models yield power estimates differing by nearly two orders of magnitude. The difference is attributed to the typically lower electron break energies in FSRQs, and the dominance of external Compton processes reduces sensitivity to particle energy distribution assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The jet power estimates in FSRQs are relatively insensitive to the choice of particle energy distribution model, unlike in HBLs. This insensitivity reflects the dominance of external Compton emission mechanisms and lower electron break energies in FSRQs, making spectral curvature less impactful on power estimates.

title: Double-Adiabatic Equations of State for Relativistic Plasmas
summary: The adiabatic equation of state $P \propto n^Γ$ describes the pressure evolution of highly collisional, isotropic plasmas in terms of their density, providing a possible closure of the fluid moment hierarchy in the absence of heat fluxes and dissipation. An analogous closure exists for collisionless, magnetised plasmas, whose pressure tensor is anisotropic with respect to the magnetic field, and the closure is therefore double-adiabatic, prescribing the evolution of the parallel and perpendicular pressures in terms of the magnetic-field strength and density. Here, we present a general first-principle formalism to derive adiabatic laws using the symmetries of the system. With this theory we recover the adiabatic equation of state $P \propto n^Γ$ for isotropic plasmas and the double-adiabatic equations of state for collisionless, magnetised plasmas. We extend the latter to the relativistic regime, finding that their exact functional form depends on the pressure anisotropy and is not a simple power law. Our double-adiabatic equations of state describe simple geometries, like magnetic mirrors or compressed homogeneous plasmas, as well as complex high-energy astrophysical processes, such as the evolution of plasmoid structures formed during magnetic reconnection.

AI.tldr: A symmetry-based formalism is developed to derive adiabatic equations of state for plasmas, recovering known isotropic and double-adiabatic forms and extending them into the relativistic regime where pressure anisotropy induces complex behavior; applicable to various plasma geometries and astrophysical phenomena.
AI.motivation: To provide a general first-principle framework deriving adiabatic laws governing pressure evolution in plasmas, including extensions to relativistic regimes.
AI.method: Developing a formalism based on the symmetries of plasma systems to recover known adiabatic equations of state and derive new generalized forms, particularly for collisionless magnetized plasmas in relativistic contexts.
AI.result: Recovered classical adiabatic and double-adiabatic equations of state for isotropic and anisotropic plasmas, respectively; extended double-adiabatic closure to relativistic plasmas revealing non-power-law dependencies on pressure anisotropy; applied the theory to both simple plasma geometries and complex astrophysical scenarios like magnetic reconnection plasmoids.
AI.conclusion: The presented symmetry-based formalism successfully unifies and extends adiabatic closures in plasma physics, enabling accurate description of pressure evolution in both isotropic and anisotropic plasmas across non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, with implications for modeling diverse plasma environments.
